failure_modes: Endogenous capture signal reflects non-EV complexes (lipoproteins, protein aggregates, or exomere-like particles) that (a) co-elute with particle peaks and (b) bind capture reagents directly or via associated ligands, producing apparent multi-epitope positivity despite lacking a membrane-protected EV—detergent/protease conditions selected are insufficiently discriminating for those complexes.

Spike-in mismatch: the exogenous intact-EV spike-in is biophysically dissimilar to endogenous EVs (different source, size, glycosylation, or surface protein density) and therefore survives device/formulation passage and protection assays while endogenous EVs are preferentially disrupted or masked; this yields a false assurance of preserved endogenous EV identity.

Assay interference by formulation/device matrices: excipients, surfactants, or high ionic-strength rinses alter antibody binding (mask/block epitopes or induce non-specific adsorption) or change fractionation behavior producing apparent preservation or loss unrelated to true EV integrity; capture-compatibility controls may not fully recapitulate matrix effects on endogenous material.

Detergent/protease/RNase treatment insufficiently discriminating or over-interpretation: chosen concentrations/incubation times fail to abolish signal from tightly associated non-vesicular complexes, or conversely overly harsh conditions destroy legitimate EVs and their signal, confounding pass/fail calls.

Particle-count co-localization misinterpretation: bulk particle counters (NTA/TRPS) detect heterogeneous particle mixtures and cannot resolve whether particle peaks represent membrane-enclosed EVs versus similarly sized non-vesicular particles; co-localization with capture signal will therefore be ambiguous.

Species- or device-specific in vivo disconnect: even if in vitro passage preserves the proposed identity gate, prior large-animal data show intranasal administration often yields negligible brain exposure—so preserving an in vitro surface phenotype may not predict in vivo delivery or justify advancing material for intranasal bridging.

Operational reproducibility limitations: fractionation and low-biomass capture detection are variable and low-throughput; inter-lot variability or limited replicate numbers (n=3) may produce stochastic pass/fail outcomes that are not robust for CMC decisions.
strongest_objection: The single strongest, bounded reason this proposal could fail is that preserved capture-signal after device/formulation passage will be driven by non-EV, capture-reactive soluble or particulate secretome components (or by reagent-buffer interactions) that co-fractionate with particle-count peaks and survive detergent/protease conditions used, so the spike-in control verifies assay function but does not exclude that endogenous capture signal is non-vesicular—i.e., the assay will produce validated-positive results while misclassifying secretome-derived material as intact EVs.
